headline: Approved projects at 35 State Road, 3 Mann Street, and 300 & 301 Barber Avenue; continued 1 & 3 Suburban Road hearing.
summary: Four projects received order conditions: 35 State Road, 3 Mann Street, 300 & 301 Barber Avenue, and 26 & 28 Milton Street. The hearing on 1 & 3 Suburban Road was continued to October 5, after residents raised concerns about soil, stormwater, and wetlands. Several other hearings were postponed, and certificates of compliance were issued for several sites.
decisions: Postponed public hearings for items 1, 4, 5, 8, 9, and 11, 4-0. Items 1, 5, 8, 9, and 11 moved to 10/05/2026, and item 4 moved to a date to be determined.
Issued a negative determination of applicability for 104 Lamartine Street, 4-0.
Issued order conditions for 35 State Road, 4-0.
Issued order conditions for 3 Mann Street, 4-0.
Issued order conditions for 300 & 301 Barber Avenue, 4-0.
Continued the public hearing for 1 & 3 Suburban Road to October 5, 2026, 4-0.
Issued order conditions for 26 & 28 Milton Street, 4-0.
Issued a partial Certificate of Compliance for Lots 1-7 Tory Fort Lane, 4-0.
Issued a partial Certificate of Compliance for 34 Bittersweet Boulevard, 4-0.
Issued a Certificate of Compliance for 115 Northeast Cutoff, 4-0.
Issued a Certificate of Compliance for 0, 9, & 19 Hemans Street, 7 Hemans Court, and 40 & 40R Milton Street, 4-0.
Issued a Certificate of Compliance for 148 Tory Fort Lane, 4-0.
Issued a certificate of compliance for 522 Grove Street, 3-0.
Ratified the emergency certificate for 320 June Street, 4-0.
Lifted the enforcement order for 570 Lincoln Street, 4-0.

Conservation Commission 
Meeting Minutes 
September 14th, 2026 
City Hall – Levi Lincoln Chamber,  
with remote participation options available via Zoom online at 
https://worcesterma.zoomgov.com/j/1604682366 and  
call-in number 1-669-254-5252 (Meeting ID: 160 468 2366). 
 
Attendance: 
Commissioners

(DPRS)

Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to postpone the public hearings as discussed.  
New Business – Request for Determination of Applicability 
2) 104 Lamartine Street (MBL 05-012-00005) – CC-2026-063 
John Garofalo of Arris Lamartine, LLC, the property owner, reviewed repairs of an existing 
paved apron accessing Sargent Street.  The work is strictly restorative, intended to make 
the entrance safe for a new tenant and pedestrian traffic. 
 
Ms. VandenBoom noted the site fell within Bordering Land Subject to Flooding, making 
Commission review necessary, but confirmed that the repair would maintain existing 
grades and create no adverse impacts.  
 
No comments from the Commission or public.      
 
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to issue a negative determination of applicability as discussed.    
List of Exhibits:  
Exhibit A: Request for Determination of Applicability; dated 08/25/2026; prepared 
by Patrick Smith, Patriot Paving   
Old Business – Notice of Intent  
4) 35 State Road (MBL 32-019-00316) - CC-2026-045 & DEP#349- 1458 
Vito Colonna, Connorstone Engineering, Inc., presented revised plans addressing concerns 
presented at a previous meeting.  The plan now incorporated pretreatment, filtration, and 
infiltration for all impervious surfaces, ensuring that routine storms up to one inch in 
volume would discharge no flow.  Only larger storms would generate overflow to a 
controlled discharge point.  Mr. Colonna also noted that wetland flags were refreshed due 
to wear over the past year.  He also requested a waiver to place riprap in the 30 ft buffer, 
citing unavoidable grade constraints and the need to access appropriate discharge 
elevation.
Mr. Flint reviewed MassDEP’s feedback confirming that infiltration is ordinarily 
prohibited in Zone A but allowed some flexibility given that the project combined 
redevelopment with new disturbance. With additional treatment between pretreatment 
and infiltration, he stated the project now met Stormwater Standard 6, applicable to 
critical areas. 
   
Commissioners questioned snow storage proximity to wetlands, salt usage, and whether 
the depicted picnic table required a platform. Commissioners also considered whether 
riprap could be relocated outside the buffer, but Mr. Colonna demonstrated that 
topography made alternative placement impossible without extensive disturbance. 
 
No comments from the public.   
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to close the public hearing.  
Only wetland flags WF-A5 - WF-A23 are confirmed by this Order of Conditions, and a 
discretionary allowance is issued under Section 4.2.4 of the Worcester Wetlands 
Protection Ordinance for the rip-rap outfall in the 30' buffer zone.     
In addition to the standard conditions, Mr. Flint recommended special conditions for 
wetland flagging, permanent markers, revised plans depicting permanent markers, 
demarcation of limit of work, stormwater management system maintenance, infiltration 
unit inspection, certification of stormwater infrastructure, wood removal, dust controls, 
dewatering, cement truck washing, equipment placement, spill prevention, as-built plan 
when request a certificate of compliance, sand/salt, snow storage, and wetland permitting.  
He recommended ongoing conditions for stormwater management system maintenance, 
sand/salt, snow storage, and wetland permitting.         
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to issue the order conditions as discussed.    
List of Exhibits:  
Exhibit A: Notice of Intent; dated 06/22/2026; prepared by Vito Colonna, 
Connorstone Engineering, Inc.    
Exhibit B: Site Plan; dated 05/21/2026; revised 06/22/2026; prepared by Vito 
Colonna, Connorstone Engineering, Inc. 
Exhibit C: Stormwater Report; dated 05/20/2026; prepared by Vito Colonna, 
Connorstone Engineering, Inc.  
Exhibit D: Wetland Report; dated 10/24/2025; Doug Dillon, Goddard Consulting 
Exhibit E: Division of Planning & Regulatory Services Comments; dated 
07/28/2026; prepared by Eric Flint & MattieVandenBoom  
 
New Business – Notice of Intent 
6) 3 Mann Street (MBL 14-033-00002) – CC-2026-058 & DEP#349-1459 
Micheal Andrade, Graves Engineering, Inc. on behalf of the applicant, Daniel Remeika, Jr., 
presented a proposal to create a second lot with a new duplex and improved off-street
parking behind an existing multifamily structure. Approximately three-quarters of the 
property lies within Bordering Land Subject to Flooding associated with Beaver Brook, 
prompting careful attention to grade changes and compensatory storage.  Mr. Andrade 
described revisions made after staff comments, including more detailed flood storage 
calculations and the addition of a second stormwater facility for roof runoff. Because soil 
testing had not originally been completed at the new infiltration location, he requested 
permission to perform confirmatory soil testing during construction and remove the unit if 
groundwater or soil proved unsuitable.   
 
Mr. Flint confirmed minor remaining comments had been addressed.  He noted that one 
bioretention basin had just under one foot of groundwater separation—below the usual 2 
ft—but acceptable under redevelopment provisions that apply “to the maximum extent 
practicable.” Staff had no objection to confirmatory test pits, citing past approvals for 
similar practices, particularly when adjacent test pit data was available.   
 
Chair Fratoni asked what would occur if soil testing revealed infiltration was infeasible.  
Mr. Andrade explained that if the second infiltration basin proved unsuitable, the roof 
runoff could instead be routed to the primary rain garden without affecting compliance.   
 
No comments from the public.   
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to close the public hearing.  
In addition to the standard conditions, Mr. Flint recommended special conditions test pit 
data, stormwater management system maintenance, infiltration unit inspection, 
certification of stormwater infrastructure, dust controls, dewatering, cement truck 
washing, spill prevention, as-built plan when requesting Certificate of Compliance, sand 
and salt, snow storage, and wetland permitting.  He recommended ongoing conditions for 
stormwater management system maintenance, sand and salt, snow storage, and wetland 
permitting.    
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to issue the order conditions as discussed. 
 
List of Exhibits:  
Exhibit A: Notice of Intent; dated 07/29/2026; prepared by Micheal Andrade, 
Graves Engineering, Inc.   
Exhibit B: Site Plan; dated 07/29/2026; revised 09/03/2026; prepared by Micheal 
Andrade, Graves Engineering, Inc.  
Exhibit C: Stormwater Report; dated 07/29/2026; prepared by Micheal Andrade, 
Graves Engineering, Inc.  
Exhibit D: Division of Planning & Regulatory Comments; dated 08/21/2026; 
prepared by Eric Flint & Mattie VandenBoom  
Exhibit E: Department of Environmental Protection; dated 08/25/2026; prepared 
by Rebecca Gendreau 
Exhibit F: Response to Comments; dated 09/04/2026; prepared by Micheal
Andrade, Graves Engineering, Inc.  
 
7) 300 & 301 Barber Avenue (MBL 22-015-00001 & 22-015-00002) - CC-2026-
059 & DEP#349-1460 
Douglas Dillon, Goddard Consulting, on behalf of the applicant, 301 Barber Avenue Owner 
LLC, explained that heavy rains earlier in the year caused approximately 100 linear feet of 
a retaining wall supporting a commercial parking lot to collapse. The proposal involved 
reconstructing the failed portion of the wall using concrete blocks, installing a gravel 
drainage column, and removing debris near the adjacent wetland.  
 
Mr. Dillon requested waivers allowing necessary work within the 15‑ft and 30‑ft buffer 
zones due to the location of the collapse and the need to remove displaced material. 
 
Mr. Dillon discussed a drainage basin that appears on site plans but clarified that it is not 
jurisdictional under the Wetlands Protection Act. Only trash removal was proposed in the 
basin and no excavation, re‑grading, or hydrologic modification are proposed.  
 
Mr. Flint noted that staff had not yet fully reviewed responses to their comment letter and 
that more time was needed to verify historical documentation associated with the basin’s 
jurisdictional status. He recommended a finding stating that the Order of Conditions 
would not confirm jurisdiction either way.  
 
Mr. Flint also sought clarification on construction access.  Mr. Dillon stated equipment 
would remain on the upper parking-lot side, with only minimal lowering of compactors 
directly from above if needed.   
 
Commissioners Canton asked questions regarding dead-man anchor installation, 
compaction techniques, and ensuring no machinery would impact undisturbed slopes.  
Mr. Dillion reviewed the dead-man anchor installation and compaction techniques 
proposed.    
 
No comments from the public. 
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to close the public hearing.  
Mr. Flint recommended the following finding that this Order of Conditions does not 
confirm the jurisdictional status of the basin or swale where trash and debris is removed.  
He also noted a discretionary allowance is issued under Section 4.2.4 of the Wetlands 
Protection Ordinance for activity within the 15' buffer zone and the reconstruction of the 
retaining wall within its existing footprint in the 30' buffer zone. 
In addition to the standard conditions, Mr. Flint recommended special conditions wetland 
flagging, dewatering, cement truck washing, equipment placement, and spill prevention. 
Upon a motion by Commissioner Kirshner, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to issue the order conditions as discussed.

Consulting LLC   
Exhibit B: Site Plan; dated 08/04/2026; revised 09/04/2026; prepared by 
Katherine A. Cruz, Hancock Associates  
Exhibit C: Stormwater Checklist; dated 09/04/2026; prepared by Katherine A. Cruz, 
Hancock Associates   
Exhibit D: Geotechnical Engineering Report; dated 08/11/2026; prepared by Nathan 
T. Davis, McPhail Associates, LLC  
Exhibit E: Division of Planning & Regulatory Comments; dated 08/24/2026; 
prepared by Eric Flint & Mattie VandenBoom  
Exhibit F: Response to Comments; dated 09/10/2026; prepared by Doug Dillon, 
Goddard Consulting LLC  
 
10)  1 & 3 Suburban Road (MBL 11-011-0002A & 43-011-0001B) - CC-2026-064 
Derek Masionis, VHB, introduced the project team, including representatives from Wood 
Partners, Jim Lambert and Kelen Araujo, and wetland scientist Scott Morrison, VHB. He 
explained that the Notice of Intent was filed solely under Worcester’s local wetlands 
ordinance, since no work was proposed within the 100‑ft buffer zone. Instead, the 
regulatory trigger was disturbance exceeding 5,000 square feet within the stormwater 
protection zone. He provided an overview of the proposed development which included 
three five‑story residential buildings totaling 300 units, 600 required parking spaces, an 
access drive from Suburban Road, a gated emergency access from Havlin Street, and 
accessory structures including a clubhouse, mail room, pool, and fire pit. He explained that 
all excavated soil would remain on site and that the originally large northern detention 
area had been significantly reduced following detailed cut‑and‑fill analysis. He described 
the overall grade as relatively flat and the stormwater design as a closed drainage system 
feeding shallow subsurface infiltration units designed to fully infiltrate the two‑year storm, 
with overflow directed to a northwest outlet structure discharging to the wetland. He 
asserted compliance with state stormwater standards and detailed erosion controls and 
construction sequencing, including clearing, bulk grading, underground utilities, 
foundation installation, binder pavement, and stabilization.  
 
Mr. Morrison described the wetland delineation, noting consistency across previous 
consultant boundaries. He explained that historical aerial photography from 1938 and 
1960 showed that material deposition and fill occurred decades before the Wetlands 
Protection Act or the city ordinance existed. He confirmed that the southern section of the 
property was maintained lawn while the northern portion was forested with steeper slopes. 
Morrison emphasized that no work was proposed within the 100-ft buffer zone and 
clarified that filing was required only because stormwater components fell within the 
locally regulated stormwater protection area. He described ongoing efforts to reduce 
clearing in the northern area and preserve more existing trees.  
 
Mr. Flint summarized staff’s comment letter noting the need for more detailed erosion 
control phasing, additional inlet protection, stockpile and temporary basin plans, and 
clearer dewatering procedures. Staff expressed concern regarding groundwater elevations 
and redox features not fully captured in some test pits and questioned whether infiltration
areas possessed suitable soils without excavation, given reports of fill depths up to 12 feet. 
He noted that because the project lies outside the buffer zone, it is reviewed strictly under 
the city’s wetlands ordinance, not the Wetlands Protection Act. 
 
Commissioner Canton asked about the building placement.  Mr. Masionis explained the 
building placement constrained by the RG-5 zoning district. 
 
Commissioner Canton expressed concern about insufficient landscape setbacks on the east 
and south sides, potential grading directing runoff toward abutting properties, and the 
need for a more robust planting plan. 
Chair Fratoni raised concerns about long-term stormwater system functionality. She 
questioned whether dozens of shallow infiltration chambers distributed across filled land 
could perform adequately and who would be responsible for future excavation or 
replacement should the systems fail.  She also expressed concern that unstable soils could 
dramatically increase construction costs and possibly lead to project abandonment, 
leaving a cleared but undeveloped site.   
D. Peterson, resident, gave philosophical and environmental objections to the project, 
questioning the Commission’s role in conservation and criticizing the elimination of 
forested land. He raised concerns about traffic congestion, quality of life impacts from 
high-rise density, and societal disconnection from nature. He asked the Commission to 
protect remaining undeveloped land and avoid destruction of wetlands and woods near 
Peat Meadow. 
Katy Silverstein, resident, provided highly technical analysis of the stormwater report, 
arguing that soil classifications used in modeling were incorrect and contradicted by the 
geotechnical logs, which showed wet clay, peat, and wet sand. These conditions she stated 
should place the soils in hydrologic group D. Using group A-C soils in modeling would 
underestimate runoff and overestimate infiltration, likely causing flooding. She also 
delivered extensive testimony asserting that the site is a historic landfill containing 
industrial waste, coal ash, petroleum-contaminated soils, tannery scraps, and drums. Her 
testimony also claimed that the peat beneath the fill continues to function as a wetland by 
storing water and filtering contaminants. She warned that excavation and oxidation of 
peat could release pollutants, undermine natural stormwater regulation, and destroy the 
remaining wet meadow. She concluded by urging the Commission to halt work, require 
removal of contaminated fill, delineate wetlands properly, and re-evaluate jurisdiction. 
Harlem Montero, resident and wetland scientist, described peat bog ecosystems as highly 
effective natural stormwater retention systems, noting their ability to hold water many 
times their weight. He emphasized the ecological value and resilience of the peat bog on 
the site and urged the Commission to protect it rather than permit additional disturbance. 
Dr. Beverly Rotar, resident, expressed concerns about human and animal health risks 
associated with disturbing contaminated soils and groundwater. She warned that wildlife 
habitat would be destroyed and raised practical concerns about already strained parking 
near Dorety High School. She cited reporting on past issues with this developer’s projects 
and urged caution.
Kim Sabrowski, resident, described the area’s long‑standing wildlife presence and her 
personal experience with clay soils and groundwater flow patterns that direct water from 
Bancroft Tower toward Peat Meadow. She warned that many neighboring homes have 
already experienced water issues and urged the Commission not to approve the 
development. 
Paula Rosenblum, resident, described discovering 10–12 feet of coal ash on her property 
while constructing an accessory dwelling unit. She said the developer’s plan does not 
include proper containment or remediation of similar fill on the site and expressed alarm 
that peat layers acting as natural filtration would be disturbed and potentially release 
toxins into surrounding neighborhoods.  
Sarah Samserian, resident, emphasized health risks and asked who would pay medical 
bills if contamination affected residents. She highlighted flooding risks, sump pump 
dependence in homes, and the lack of affordable housing in the proposal. She criticized 
Wood Partners for allegedly flipping properties quickly and raised concerns about 
responsibility for structural failures. 
Fred Nathan, resident, acknowledged the need for development but warned that 
development on wetlands has historically caused neighborhood harm. He noted other 
projects that displaced wetlands and raised concerns about rising rents and long‑term 
impacts on neighborhood stability.  
Phyllis Patrick, resident, described widespread water issues in her neighborhood and 
referenced a New York Times article about inadequate culvert capacity nationwide. She 
urged consideration of how increased stormwater might affect existing culverts, including 
one near Duffy Field. 
Richie Schoffield, resident, described discovering massive voids beneath his 115‑year‑old 
home’s slab during foundation repairs, requiring installation of 20‑foot helical piles. He 
warned that similar soil instability is likely to be present under the project site and urged 
careful evaluation.  
Alexandra, resident, stated support for neighbors’ comments and emphasized that while 
housing is needed, it should not come at the cost of harm to existing residents. She 
stressed that the proposal would cause unacceptable impacts to surrounding homes and 
ecosystems.  
Kevin Crowley, resident, stated that he grew up near the site and remembered it as “the 
swamp,” reinforcing historical claims that the area is a wetland.  
Blaine Grandstaff, resident, stated he has two sump pumps running continuously during 
rain, described chronic standing water in his yard and worries about toxic groundwater 
entering his home and yard. He said he is unconvinced that the stormwater plan will 
adequately protect neighbors.  
Marica and David Devio, residents, expressed general agreement with previous speakers 
and stated that hearing the testimony had increased their concerns.
Greg Dorsler, resident, discussed flooding issues on his side of Highland Street and 
recalled mud washing down during the Dorety High School construction project. He 
expressed concern about how the proposed northern berm—constructed from potentially 
contaminated materials—could leach pollutants into the wetlands. 
Jim Lambert of Wood Partners, the applicant, thanked the Commission and public for 
their input and stated that the applicant would review all comments, produce revised 
plans, and return prepared to respond to concerns.  
Chair Fratoni confirmed that the Commission will continue the hearing to October 5, with 
all revised materials due one week before the meeting. She reiterated the need for detailed 
clarification about soil contamination, groundwater behavior, structural feasibility, 
long-term stormwater maintenance, and assurances against site abandonment.  
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to continue the public hearing to October 5th.  
List of Exhibits:  
Exhibit A: Notice of Intent; dated 08/26/2026; prepared by Scott Morrision, VHB    
Exhibit B: Site Plan; dated 08/13/2026; prepared by Justin W. Dufrense, VHB 
Exhibit C: Stormwater Report; dated 08/13/2026; prepared by Justin W. Dufrense, 
VHB

prepared by Eric Flint & Mattie VandenBoom

Exhibit G: Public Comment; dated 09/09/2026; prepared by Katy Silverstein 
Exhibit H: Public Comment; dated 09/14/2026; prepared by Elaine Baskin 
 
12) 26 & 28 Milton Street (MBL 09-028-19-22 & 09-028-1922A) - CC-2026-066 
Joseph Graham, project engineer, explained that the project team had been brought in 
after construction on two three-unit buildings had already begun without proper 
Conservation Commission filings. The roadway had been base-paved, utilities installed, 
and structures largely completed before the Conservation process began. The applicant has 
now sought approval of corrective plans designed to bring the project back into 
compliance.  
 
Mr. Flint noted the late submission of some materials but found that most technical 
comments had been addressed.  A mounding analysis due to proximity of groundwater to 
infiltration systems, and a revised planting plan using at least 50% native species are still 
required but can be conditioned into the Order of Conditions.   
 
Chair Fratoni asked about the sequence for the remainder of the work.  Mr. Graham 
explained that the remaining items include installation of two catch basins on the private 
road, construction of infiltration units in the driveways, and landscaping.  He expects the 
work to be completed by winter.
No comments from the public. 
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Nystrom, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to close the public hearing.  
In addition to the standard conditions, Mr. Flint recommended special conditions to 
provide mounding analysis, stormwater management system maintenance, infiltration 
unit inspection, certification of stormwater infrastructure, dust controls, dewatering, 
cement truck washing, spill prevention, as-built plan when requesting Certificate of 
Compliance, and sand and salt.  He recommended ongoing conditions for stormwater 
management system maintenance and sand and salt.  
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to issue the order conditions as discussed.  
List of Exhibits:  
Exhibit A: Notice of Intent; dated 08/26/2026; prepared by Joseph Graham, EJ

Other Business 
13)   Request for Certificate of Compliance 
a. Lots 1-7 Tory Fort Lane (CC-2005-038 & DEP# 349-0837) 
Ms. VandenBoom explained a partial certificate is requested for an older 2005 filing 
affecting land later developed for a single-family home. As no work from the original filing 
impacted the present lot, she recommended issued a partial certificate of compliance.    
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Nystrom, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to issue the partial Certificate of Compliance. 
b. 34 Bittersweet Boulevard (CC-2009-042 & DEP#349-0979)  
Ms. VandenBoom explained that a partial Certificate of Compliance was being requested 
for one side of a duplex within the Arboretum subdivision.   She confirmed the site was 
fully stabilized. 
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to issue a partial Certificate of Compliance. 
c. 115 Northeast Cutoff (CC-2022-004 & DEP# 349-1314)  
Patrick Healey of Thompson-Liston Associates requested a Certificate of Compliance for 
the school bus parking area that included wetland crossing and replication area. He
reported that all work is complete, the site is fully stabilized, and the replication area has 
been constructed and is functioning properly. The Conservation Restriction has been 
signed by the City of Worcester and the Commonwealth, recorded at the Registry of Deeds, 
and the associated transfer is complete. Staff confirmed the site conditions and had no 
remaining concerns. 
   
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Nystrom, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to issue the Certificate of Compliance. 
d. 0, 9, & 19 Hemans Street, 7 Hemans Court, and 40 & 40R Milton Street (CC-
2022-032)  
Ms. VandenBoom reported that the residential low-rise construction site is complete and 
fully stabilized. An as-built plan and engineering certification confirm proper stormwater 
function. 
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the 
Commission voted 4-0 to issue a Certificate of Compliance. 
e. 148 Tory Fort Lane (CC-2023-016 & DEP#349-1356)  
Ms. VandenBoom explained this project involved construction of a single-family home.  
Staff inspected the site and confirmed that permanent markers have been installed and the 
site is stabilized. An enforcement order remains open pending receipt of the final 
monitoring report. 
Upon a motion by Commissioner Canton, seconded by Commissioner Kirshner, the
